theme: Obey the law; the Ten Commandments repeated
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 4:1-5:33. Moses turns from history to instruction. He urges Israel to obey, and he restates the Ten Commandments. Notice the reasons he gives for obedience.
settingTheScene: Having reviewed the journey, Moses begins his second major address. The word “now” in 4:1 marks the turn: “And now, O Israel, listen to the statutes and the rules that I am teaching you.” He wants the people to keep the law carefully, because it is their wisdom before the nations. Then, in chapter 5, he gathers the whole assembly and repeats the Ten Commandments given at Horeb, with some variations from the version in Exodus.
observation: “You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it” (4:2).
“Keep them and do them, for that will be your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples” (4:6).
“For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the LORD our God is to us, whenever we call upon him?” (4:7).
“You saw no form on the day that the LORD spoke to you at Horeb out of the midst of the fire” (4:15).
“The LORD your God is a merciful God. He will not leave you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers” (4:31).
“Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the rules that I speak in your hearing today” (5:1).
The Ten Commandments are given again (5:6-21), with the Sabbath commandment grounded in the exodus: “You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (5:15).
The people say, “Go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say… and we will hear and do it” (5:27).
interpretation:
Moses begins with a startling claim: the law is a gift that makes Israel the envy of the nations. The nations will hear these statutes and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people.” Obedience is not a burden but a witness. The law shows what a people ruled by a just and loving God would look like.

The reason is not just the laws, but the God who gave them. “What great nation has a god so near to it?” The nearness of God is the glory of Israel. The other nations had gods to be placated from afar. Israel’s God spoke from the fire and called them to himself.

Moses warns against making images. At Horeb, the people heard a voice, but they saw no form. That was deliberate. A God who cannot be pictured cannot be controlled. Moses stresses that the temptation to make an image, to shape God into something we can handle, is real, and he warns of the consequences.

The restatement of the Ten Commandments in chapter 5 shows how the law was meant to be internalized. The same words that were spoken to the previous generation are now spoken to the next, in the present tense: “The LORD made this covenant not with our fathers but with us, who are all of us here alive today” (5:3). Each generation must receive the covenant as its own.

One difference from Exodus is that the Sabbath commandment gives a new reason. In Exodus, it is based on creation. Here, it is based on redemption: “You shall remember that you were a slave.” The Sabbath is a gift to those who were once denied rest, and it extends rest to servants and animals.

The people’s response sounds right. “We will hear and do it.” But God says that he wishes they had such a heart always. Hearing and doing are the key, and the whole book will keep returning to them.
connection: Jesus said, “Think not that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). He is the visible image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), the “form” that Israel did not see. Paul says that the law was a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24). Jesus says, “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15).
application:
Read the Ten Commandments aloud slowly. Ask which one the Spirit is pressing on you this week.

Think about how your life displays the wisdom of God to those around you.

Thank God that he is near, and that you can call upon him at any time.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he has drawn near in Jesus.
Ask him to write his commandments on your heart.
Ask him to let your obedience be a witness to those around you.
